tour.overview:
In the 15th century, Florence was a city of bankers, wool merchants and craftsmen who paid for art the way other cities paid for armies. Under the Medici family, Brunelleschi raised the largest dome since antiquity, Botticelli painted Venus rising from the sea, and the young Michelangelo carved David from a block of marble that other sculptors had given up on. The historic centre of Florence has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1982.

This private day puts the masterpieces in order with a licensed guide, so you understand how the Renaissance began, not just where it hangs. You see Michelangelo's David first thing in the morning, before the queues, then the cathedral square with its dome, bell tower and Baptistery. After a Tuscan lunch, you walk through Piazza della Signoria to the Uffizi, cross the Ponte Vecchio and end the day with the view from Piazzale Michelangelo, reached by car.

AT A GLANCE
• Duration: about 8 hours
• Start and end: your hotel in Florence
• Type: private walking tour with licensed guide; car for the final viewpoint and the return
• Booking: on request – we confirm availability and the final price by email within 24 hours, and you pay only then
• Level: easy; about 5 km on flat paving in the historic centre

WHAT YOU SEE
• The Accademia Gallery and Michelangelo's David.
• The Duomo, Giotto's bell tower and the Baptistery (outside; the cathedral interior when open).
• Piazza della Signoria, Palazzo Vecchio and the Loggia dei Lanzi.
• The Uffizi Gallery.
• The Ponte Vecchio.
• Piazzale Michelangelo.

WHY THIS WORKS
We book the first David entry of the day and an early-afternoon Uffizi slot, when the morning groups have left, and keep the walks short between them.

WHO IT SUITS
First-time visitors to Florence, art lovers, and families who want the highlights explained in a lively way.

WHO MAY PREFER ANOTHER TOUR
If you have seen the museums before and want the countryside, choose our Chianti, San Gimignano and Siena day trip.

PRACTICAL INFORMATION
The Accademia and the Uffizi are closed on Mondays. Climbing the dome (463 steps) needs a separate timed ticket that sells out weeks ahead; ask when you book. Florence is very hot in July and August.

days.name: Michelangelo's David, the Duomo and Baptistery, Piazza della Signoria, the Uffizi, Ponte Vecchio and Piazzale Michelangelo
days.description:
What to expect: the masterpieces of the Renaissance in one well-paced day, with a licensed guide, timed tickets, lunch and a car for the final viewpoint.

Your guide meets you at your hotel at about 8:15 and walks you to the Accademia Gallery for one of the first entries of the day. Along a corridor lined with Michelangelo's unfinished Prisoners, figures still struggling out of the marble, you reach the tribune where David stands, 5.17 metres tall. Michelangelo carved him between 1501 and 1504, aged 26, from a block that had lain abandoned for decades, and the Florentines placed him in front of their town hall as a symbol of the small republic standing up to its powerful enemies.

A short walk brings you to the Piazza del Duomo. The cathedral of Santa Maria del Fiore is clad in white, green and pink marble, and its dome, built by Filippo Brunelleschi between 1420 and 1436 without a supporting frame, is still the largest brick dome in the world. Beside it rises Giotto's bell tower, and in front stands the octagonal Baptistery, with Lorenzo Ghiberti's gilded bronze doors that Michelangelo called the Gates of Paradise. When the cathedral is open, you step inside to see the frescoed Last Judgment under the dome.

After lunch at a trattoria near the Central Market – ribollita soup, pappardelle with wild boar or a bistecca if you are hungry – you walk to Piazza della Signoria, the political heart of the city, with the fortress-like Palazzo Vecchio and the statues of the Loggia dei Lanzi, among them Cellini's Perseus. Next door, in the Uffizi, the Medici offices turned into one of the oldest museums in Europe, your guide leads you to Giotto, Botticelli's Birth of Venus and Primavera, Leonardo da Vinci's Annunciation, Michelangelo's Doni Tondo, Raphael and Caravaggio. From the Uffizi windows you look onto the Ponte Vecchio, which you then cross, its shops held by goldsmiths since 1593 under the hidden corridor that the Medici used to move between their palaces. Your car takes you up to Piazzale Michelangelo for the view over the domes and towers of Florence before driving you back to your hotel at about 17:00.

SCHEDULE (approximate times)
08:15 – Meeting at your hotel.
08:30 – Accademia Gallery and David (about 1 hour 15 minutes).
10:00 – Piazza del Duomo: cathedral, bell tower and Baptistery.
11:30 – Walk through the medieval centre and the Central Market.
12:30 – Lunch in a trattoria.
14:00 – Piazza della Signoria and the Loggia dei Lanzi.
14:30 – Uffizi Gallery (about 2 hours).
16:30 – Ponte Vecchio and car to Piazzale Michelangelo.
17:00 – Back at your hotel.

GOOD TO KNOW
• The Accademia and the Uffizi are closed on Mondays; on that day we visit the Bargello or the Medici Chapels instead.
• The dome climb and Giotto's bell tower need separate timed tickets; ask us when booking.
• The cathedral interior has a long free queue; your guide decides on the day whether it is worth it.

INCLUDED: licensed guide, Accademia and Uffizi tickets, lunch, car to Piazzale Michelangelo and back to your hotel, bottled water.
NOT INCLUDED: dome climb and bell tower, drinks with lunch, tips.

Overnight: none.
Meals: lunch.

faq.question: How does booking on request work?
faq.answer: You choose a date and the number of travellers and send the request. Nothing is charged. We confirm availability and the final price by email within 24 hours, and you pay online only when the tour is confirmed.

faq.question: Do we skip the lines?
faq.answer: Yes. We book timed tickets for the Accademia and the Uffizi, so you skip the ticket lines, which can be over an hour in season. There is a short security check for everyone.

faq.question: Is the tour possible on Mondays?
faq.answer: The Accademia and the Uffizi are closed on Mondays. On a Monday we replace them with the Bargello, with Donatello's David, and the Medici Chapels, with Michelangelo's tombs.

faq.question: Can we climb the dome?
faq.answer: Yes, if tickets are available. The climb has 463 steps on narrow stairs and timed tickets sell out weeks ahead in season, so ask us when you book.

faq.question: Are the entrance tickets included?
faq.answer: Yes: the Accademia Gallery and the Uffizi Gallery. The Duomo is free to enter; the dome, bell tower and Baptistery interior need extra tickets.

faq.question: Is there much walking?
faq.answer: About 5 km on flat paving. The historic centre is mostly pedestrian, so we walk between the sights and use the car for Piazzale Michelangelo and the return.

faq.question: Is lunch included?
faq.answer: Yes, a Tuscan lunch at a trattoria. Vegetarian, gluten-free and other diets can be arranged.

faq.question: Is it suitable for children?
faq.answer: Yes. We turn the museums into a treasure hunt and keep the visits short. Children usually love David, the bridge and the view at the end.

faq.question: Is it suitable for people with limited mobility?
faq.answer: Largely. The Accademia and the Uffizi have lifts, and the centre is flat. Some pavements are narrow and cobbled. Tell us your needs and we will adapt.

faq.question: Can we take photos?
faq.answer: Yes, without flash, in the Accademia and the Uffizi, including David. Selfie sticks and tripods are not allowed.

faq.question: What should we wear?
faq.answer: Comfortable shoes and, for the cathedral, clothes covering shoulders and knees.

faq.question: What is the best time of year?
faq.answer: April to early June and September to October. July and August are hot and very busy; winter is quiet and the museums are at their most enjoyable.

faq.question: What is the cancellation policy?
faq.answer: You can cancel free of charge up to 72 hours before the tour, because museum tickets are non-refundable after that. Until your request is confirmed, nothing is charged at all.
